final.title: Subprocessor lists are part of the workflow design
final.body:
If you are running a 1–10-person business and you are thinking about automating a workflow that touches customer data, the subprocessor list is not a footnote. It is part of the design. The question is plain: which third parties will see the data, at which step, and for what purpose?

Start with one recurring workflow only: invoice handling, customer inquiries, or document storage. Pick the one where data already passes through the most hands. Then write down the current handlers in order: your team, the SaaS tools you already use, any vendor, and any consultant. Note where each handoff happens and whether that step already has a data-processing agreement. That is the diagnostic. It is not glamorous, but it keeps the build honest.

From there, ask whether automation would reduce the number of people or tools that can see the data. A good target is not “faster at any cost”; it is fewer access points, clearer logging, and human approval where the risk is real. For example, a controlled system can extract data, flag exceptions for review, and keep an audit trail. It should not make money movements or other high-risk decisions on its own.

If you build a pilot, define the subprocessor list up front: which tools handle data, what each one does, and where you need human sign-off before any transfer or integration starts. Put that into the pilot scope before the build, not after the surprise. That usually saves a late spreadsheet scramble.

critic_repairs.instruction: Replace the multinational/enterprise framing with the intended small-business owner-operator audience, and restate the first-step guidance for one owner-run workflow decision (for example, one recurring workflow in a 1–10 person business).

Remove the unsupported approval-specific claim about what customer approval is needed before data transfers; keep the next step limited to mapping who touches the data, which tools handle it, and where the handoffs are.
